Question: If \[ \begin{aligned} s={}&(1+2^{-\frac{1}{32}})(1+2^{-\frac{1}{16}})\\ &\cdot(1+2^{-\frac{1}{8}})(1+2^{-\frac{1}{4}})\\ &\cdot(1+2^{-\frac{1}{2}}), \end{aligned} \] then \(s\) is equal to:
Solution:
The exponents double from one factor to the next, suggesting repeated use of \((1-u)(1+u)=1-u^2\). Let
\[
t=2^{-1/32}.
\]
Then \(0<t<1\), and the product becomes
\[
s=(1+t)(1+t^2)(1+t^4)(1+t^8)(1+t^{16}).
\]
Multiplying by \(1-t\) makes the first two factors a difference of squares. The resulting factor combines with the next one in the same way:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-t)s
&=(1-t^2)(1+t^2)(1+t^4)(1+t^8)(1+t^{16})\\
&=(1-t^4)(1+t^4)(1+t^8)(1+t^{16})\\
&=1-t^{32}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the last line continues the same identity through the remaining factors. Since \(t^{32}=2^{-1}=\tfrac12\), we obtain \((1-t)s=\tfrac12\). Also \(1-t>0\), so division is valid:
\[
s=\boxed{\frac{1}{2(1-2^{-1/32})}}.
\]
This is choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
